Newborn Care

Argan oil while breastfeeding: skin, hair, food and infant contact

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Breastfeeding does not mean giving up all skin or hair care. With argan oil, however, a cosmetic benefit, suitability as food and safety on a nipple are different questions. Check the complete product and where it will be used rather than relying on the words natural or pure.

What argan oil is

Argan oil comes from the oil-rich kernels inside the hard fruit stone of the argan tree, associated especially with Morocco and neighbouring north-west Africa. Labels and studies commonly use Argania spinosa; Kew currently accepts Sideroxylon spinosum as the botanical name. The oil is a fixed plant oil, not an essential oil, although a finished cosmetic may contain added essential oils or fragrance.

Culinary oil is commonly made from roasted kernels, while cosmetic oil is commonly made from unroasted kernels. Processing changes smell, colour and composition, but a golden colour or mild aroma cannot authenticate a bottle or make it edible. Morocco's Arganeraie became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1998; that designation concerns an ecosystem, not proof of a product's purity, medical benefits or breastfeeding safety.

Nutrients without the miracle claims

Argan oil consists mainly of fat, particularly oleic acid and linoleic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid. It also contains tocopherols, forms of vitamin E, and smaller amounts of other compounds, with variation between oils and processing methods. It should not be described as a rich omega-3 source or a complete vitamin-and-mineral supplement.

Finding antioxidant compounds in a laboratory does not show that applying or eating the oil prevents DNA damage, cancer or disease in a parent or baby. Claims about carotene, vitamin A, minerals or a uniquely powerful antioxidant blend need actual product data. Oil is not a substitute for a varied diet or supplements prescribed for a deficiency.

Skin exposure is not the same as milk exposure

The claim that everything put on the skin passes into breast milk is incorrect. Many topical products have limited absorption, but exposure depends on the ingredients, amount, area, frequency and condition of the skin. A cosmetic mixture must be assessed as a mixture, not declared suitable because it contains argan oil.

A baby can also lick or touch residue directly, without it ever passing through milk. Intact skin away from the breast is a different setting from cracked nipples or a product on the hands, lips or chest that the baby mouths. Argan-specific milk-level and infant-outcome evidence is insufficient to promise safety for every route or product; it also does not establish that one incidental use has harmed a baby.

Moisture, softness and the limits of skin studies

An oil may soften the surface of dry skin and make it feel smoother. Small argan studies measured hydration or elasticity over about 60 days in 60 postmenopausal women, including application to forearms. Those findings concern selected adult skin measurements, not breastfeeding parents, cracked nipples, infant exposure or a guarantee of wrinkle prevention.

Dry cuticles, nails, heels and lips are often mentioned alongside body skin. These are cosmetic uses, not proof that argan repairs nails or heals deep cracks. Persistent painful fissures, spreading inflammation or a lip or skin lesion that does not heal deserves assessment. A simple fragrance-free moisturiser may be another option; an expensive oil is not necessary for everyone.

Hair conditioning is different from stopping postpartum shedding

Argan products may change how hair feels or looks, including shine, softness or frizz. A 2022 laboratory study found less protein loss in cut human hair pretreated before oxidative damage. That is not a clinical trial showing thicker hair, repaired split ends, prevention of breakage in everyday use or regrowth after childbirth.

Postpartum shedding often follows hormonal changes and usually improves with time; it is not proof that breastfeeding has depleted the hair. Argan oil is not an established treatment for this process, dandruff, scalp infection or persistent itching. Seek assessment for patchy loss, an inflamed scalp or shedding that is not recovering rather than repeatedly adding products.

Stretch marks, acne, pigment and wounds

Moisturising and a temporary smoother appearance are not established prevention or treatment of stretch marks, scars, age spots, uneven pigmentation, acne or excess oiliness. Anti-ageing, exfoliation and skin-renewal promises also go beyond the limited measurements in the available studies. Persistent skin changes need an appropriate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Laboratory antimicrobial or antioxidant findings do not make argan oil a disinfectant, an antiviral or an antifungal treatment, or a proven way to heal wounds and burns. Do not put it on a burn or an infected wound instead of obtaining care. It is not a tested sunscreen: keep suitable sun protection, including a labelled broad-spectrum sunscreen, clothing and shade.

Eating the oil is a separate choice

Only use a product specifically sold as food for culinary purposes. A hair serum or cosmetic oil may contain ingredients that should not be swallowed, even if its main ingredient is argan. Food oil contributes dietary fat and energy; there is no established breastfeeding dose, milk-supply benefit or reason to drink it as a treatment.

Small adult studies have investigated cholesterol and related blood markers; one short trial involved 39 adults with abnormal lipids. Such results do not establish prevention of heart attacks, treatment of diabetes or cancer, or benefit to a breastfed baby. Do not replace prescribed medicines or a clinical nutrition plan with oil, and have supplement-style use checked with a pharmacist or clinician.

Do not assume it treats cracked nipples

There is not adequate argan-specific evidence to recommend it routinely for sore, dry or cracked nipples. Removing oil before a feed does not establish that the product is suitable or that the cause of pain has been treated. Ask a midwife, breastfeeding specialist or clinician to observe a feed and assess attachment, skin irritation, pump-related injury or infection as appropriate.

If a professional recommends a particular nipple preparation, follow its product-specific directions, including any gentle removal of visible residue before feeding. Do not scrub the nipple or repeatedly wash it with soap to remove a cosmetic. Keep unassessed argan products off the nipple and areola, and do not put them on the baby as a way to test tolerance.

Practical checks for ordinary cosmetic use

Read the full ingredient list, intended use and storage instructions. Choose a clearly identified product rather than an unlabelled blend; pure is not an allergy guarantee. Keep it out of children's reach. Avoid applying a new cosmetic to broken or inflamed skin without advice, and stop if it causes irritation rather than continuing because it is marketed as healing.

Keep treated skin and oily hands from the baby's mouth and eyes, and wash your hands after application when needed to prevent transfer. Consider contact from hair products, lip products and the upper chest as well as the breast itself. If the baby has already contacted a product, keep the packaging and ask for advice about that exact exposure; do not invent a milk-discarding or feeding-interruption schedule.

Possible reactions and symptoms not to dismiss

Irritation, rash or allergy can occur. A published case describes anaphylaxis after topical argan products in an adult. A serious allergic reaction is therefore possible after skin application. A case report cannot tell us how often this happens. Avoid a product that previously caused a reaction; do not repeat a home skin or swallowing challenge to prove it is safe.

Nausea, gas or diarrhoea after eating an oil may reflect intolerance or another cause and should be assessed if persistent or troublesome. The source's list of confusion, sleep disturbance, weakness and depression is not an established argan-specific adverse-effect profile. New neurological symptoms or significant mood changes deserve care in their own right, rather than either blaming the oil automatically or ignoring them.

When feeding or breast symptoms need help

Seek feeding support promptly for pain at every feed, cracked or bleeding nipples, or difficulty keeping feeding comfortable. A hot, swollen or painful breast, a new hard area or fever and flu-like symptoms can be mastitis rather than dry skin. Do not treat it with oil or forceful massage; contact the care team, particularly if symptoms worsen or do not improve.

If a baby develops a rash, repeated vomiting or difficulty feeding after possible product contact, ask the baby's clinician promptly and keep the label. Call emergency services for breathing problems, swelling, abnormal colour, limpness or poor responsiveness as described below. These symptoms need assessment; timing after an oil does not by itself establish the cause.

Emergency reactions and suspected harmful swallowing

Get emergency help for sudden lip, mouth, tongue or throat swelling, breathing difficulty, a tight throat or difficulty swallowing, blue, grey or unusually pale colour, fainting or loss of consciousness, or sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness after a possible allergic exposure. A baby becoming limp or not responding normally is also an emergency. Do not wait for a rash or every sign. Use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if available, call an ambulance and follow emergency instructions; do not stand or walk around or drive yourself.

If an adult or child may have swallowed a harmful cosmetic or other substance, seek immediate emergency or poison-service advice without waiting for symptoms; if unsure whether it is harmful, obtain urgent poison advice. Keep the container. For suspected poisoning, do not induce vomiting or give anything to eat or drink while awaiting medical advice. Ordinary edible oil used as food is a different situation from swallowing an unknown cosmetic.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the exact product label and explain whether you want food, hair, skin or nipple use; ask about infant contact separately from milk transfer.

Ask for a feeding assessment for painful or cracked nipples rather than trying successive cosmetic oils.

Record any reaction and the timing, stop the suspected product and use the appropriate urgent or emergency contact route.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise a label photo or ingredient list, route and site of use, amount and time, symptoms, feeding observations and questions for your clinician. It cannot verify purity, decide that an oil is safe in milk or on a nipple, diagnose an allergy or replace care. Recording must not delay emergency help.

When to seek help

Keep unassessed cosmetics off nipples and infant contact areas. Seek prompt feeding help for cracked or bleeding nipples or painful feeds. Sudden mouth/throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, blue/grey/unusually pale colour, fainting or loss of consciousness, sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness, or a limp or poorly responsive baby needs emergency help; do not wait for every sign. Use prescribed adrenaline if available and call an ambulance; do not walk around or drive yourself. Suspected harmful cosmetic swallowing needs immediate advice; do not induce vomiting or give food or drink while awaiting medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Food oil, cosmetic mixtures and nipple products require different decisions.
  • Limited skin or laboratory hair findings do not establish breastfeeding safety or a cure.
  • Many topical products have low absorption; direct infant contact is a separate exposure.
  • Cracked nipples and painful feeding need assessment, not an automatic argan remedy.
  • Keep labels, stop a suspected irritant and act promptly on serious reactions.

Frequently asked questions

Is argan oil safe while breastfeeding?

There is no universal answer for every product and route. A cosmetic on intact skin away from infant contact differs from food use or application to a cracked nipple. Check the ingredients and site; limited argan-specific lactation evidence does not justify either a blanket safety promise or assuming an incidental use has caused harm.

Can it cause side effects?

Skin irritation and allergic reactions are possible, including a reported serious reaction after topical use. Digestive symptoms after eating it need assessment if persistent. Confusion, weakness, sleep or mood changes should not be labelled an established argan effect or dismissed; seek appropriate care.

Which benefits are actually supported?

Limited adult studies suggest effects on skin hydration or elasticity, while a cut-hair experiment found less oxidative damage. They do not prove treatment of postpartum shedding, cracked nipples, burns, acne, stretch marks, diabetes or cancer, or prevention of heart disease.

Which nutrients does it contain?

It is mainly fat, including oleic and linoleic acids, with tocopherols and smaller amounts of other compounds. Composition varies. It is not a rich omega-3 source or a complete vitamin-and-mineral supplement, and antioxidant content is not a medical benefit guarantee.

May I put it on a cracked nipple if I wash it off?

Do not assume that makes it suitable. Argan is not an established cracked-nipple treatment. Get feeding and skin assessment; use a professionally recommended preparation with its exact directions. Avoid harsh soap or scrubbing, and keep unassessed cosmetics off the nipple and areola.

Can I swallow the oil sold for my hair?

No. Only a product specifically sold as food belongs in food use; cosmetic formulations may contain unsuitable ingredients. If a potentially harmful product has been swallowed, get immediate advice with the label. Do not induce vomiting or give food or drink while awaiting advice for suspected poisoning.

Can BeMama help me keep track?

Record the product and ingredient list, whether it was eaten or applied, the site, amount and time, symptoms and feeding concerns, and questions for the care team. BeMama cannot authenticate oil, establish lactation safety, diagnose an allergy or nipple problem, or replace urgent assessment.

When is a reaction an emergency?

Sudden mouth or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, blue/grey/unusually pale colour, fainting or loss of consciousness, or sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness after exposure needs emergency help. A limp or poorly responsive baby also needs emergency help. Use a prescribed adrenaline injector if available, call an ambulance, do not walk around or drive yourself, and do not wait for all signs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
